active_themes.label: AI Spending Backlash
active_themes.summary: The Nasdaq fell 0.39% to 25,366 but held above the 25,000 line even as the 10-year closed above 5%. That is a better test result than feared, though small caps took the damage instead. The open question is whether 25,000 survives if yields keep climbing and Nvidia's leadership questions stay unresolved.

active_themes.label: Fed Eyes Another Hike
active_themes.summary: The dollar index rose 0.25% to 103.17, near a 19-month high, as hike bets grew, while gold fell 2.88%. Higher oil and higher yields are reinforcing each other. The open question is whether the dollar reaches 103.50, which would show markets adding further to hike bets.

active_themes.label: Iran War Resumption Risk
active_themes.summary: Brent jumped 3.3% to $95.82 after Iran's Guards said they targeted a US early-warning radar in Bahrain, so the bounce has now crossed $95. Oil is still on track for a second weekly decline, so one close above $95 is not yet a pattern. The open question is whether Brent closes above $95 again and whether more strikes follow.

active_themes.label: Global Borrowing Costs Climb
active_themes.summary: The 10-year Treasury yield closed at 5.10% (up 0.11 points) and the 30-year at 5.43% (up 0.08), clearing both lines the market was watching. Yields are being pushed by Fed hike bets and a rebound in oil at the same time. The open question is whether 10-year yields keep climbing toward 5.25% or slip back under 5.00%.

active_themes.label: Gulf Oil Slowly Returns
active_themes.summary: Brent slipped 1.17% to $91.49 and WTI 0.93% to $86.04, extending oil's slide to its lowest levels since August as shipping through Hormuz normalizes. Cheaper oil is now cushioning the inflation print rather than fixing it. The open question is whether Brent stays under $95 if another shipping incident hits.

active_themes.label: Democratic Sweep Reaction
active_themes.summary: The Democratic sweep first read as relief, then as a regulatory threat to AI. Today's tech bounce suggests part of that fear was overdone, but nothing in policy has changed. The open question is whether tech's losses outweigh the relief elsewhere, and a Senate Banking Committee led by Elizabeth Warren from January adds a new regulatory pressure point for financial firms.
